modules.name: Clock
modules.header:
Precise time, and the two clocks worth telling apart.
`QueryPerformanceCounter` is the monotonic one: it counts at a fixed rate from an arbitrary point and never goes
backwards, which makes it what a duration is measured with. Its unit is not seconds and not fixed across machines,
so a count means nothing until it is divided by `QueryPerformanceFrequency`, which is constant while the system
runs and only has to be read once.
`GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime` is the wall clock: 100-nanosecond ticks since 1601, which can jump when the
system clock is set. It is what a timestamp anyone else will see is taken from, and never what a duration is
measured with.

modules.name: Constants
modules.header:
Win32's enumerated constants, under the spellings Microsoft's documentation uses.
These are values a caller passes to the entry points in the other modules. Each keeps its published name and
value; nothing here is reinterpreted or renamed.

modules.name: Entropy
modules.header:
Unpredictable bytes, from the system's cryptographic provider.
`BCryptGenRandom` is the supported source on Windows, and the only one here fit for a key, a token, or anything an
adversary would like to guess. It lives in `bcrypt.dll` rather than in Kernel32, and reports failure as an
`NtStatus` rather than through `GetLastError` — two departures from the rest of this package that come from its
being part of the cryptographic interface rather than the kernel one.
The older `RtlGenRandom`, sometimes reached as `SystemFunction036`, is not declared here: it is undocumented as an
export, has no supported name, and Microsoft's guidance is to use this instead.

modules.name: Errors
modules.header:
The error codes `GetLastError` reports, and what reports them.
Win32 has three unrelated ways of saying something failed, and reading one as another is a common mistake. A call
returning a `Bool` or a handle reports through `GetLastError`, whose codes are these. A call in the cryptographic
or native interface reports an `NtStatus` instead, which shares no numbering with these at all. And a C runtime
call sets `errno`, which is a third scheme again.
`GetLastError` is per thread and is **not** cleared by a call that succeeds, so a code read at any moment other
than immediately after a failure is left over from something earlier.
Only the codes a caller is likely to branch on are named. There are thousands, and a program that needs one this
module does not have should compare the number rather than wait for it to appear here.

modules.name: File
modules.header:
The Unicode file and device interface.
Every entry point here is the `W` form, which takes UTF-16. The `A` forms in `Kernel` convert through the process
code page, which is lossy for any name the page cannot express and differs between machines — so a path that
works on one system fails on another for reasons the program cannot see. A path is not text the program chose; it
is text a user or a file system chose, and the `W` forms are the only ones that carry all of it.
A failing call here reports `InvalidHandleValue` where it returns a handle and zero where it returns a `Bool`,
with the reason in `GetLastError`.

modules.name: Kernel
modules.header:
The Kernel32 entry points this package binds, under the exact symbols the library exports.
A call reports failure the way Win32 does: a `Bool` of zero, a null pointer, or `InvalidHandleValue`,
depending on what it returns. The reason is then in `GetLastError`, which is per thread and is not cleared by
a successful call — so it means something only immediately after a failure.

modules.name: Memory
modules.header:
Virtual memory: reserving and committing address space, and changing what may be done with it.
Windows separates two things every other supported system runs together. Reserving takes address space without
backing it; committing gives the reserved range storage. A single call may do both, and an allocator that wants a
large arena without paying for it up front does them separately.
A failing call here reports null rather than `InvalidHandleValue`, which is the opposite of the file interface.
The reason is in `GetLastError`.

modules.name: Types
modules.header:
The Win32 ABI's fundamental types, handles and structures.
Every name here is Win32's own, because that is what a reader porting code or reading Microsoft's documentation
will look for. A `HANDLE` is an opaque pointer-sized value the kernel owns; nothing here interprets one, and the
only thing a caller may do with it is pass it back or close it.
The two invalid values are not the same. A handle-returning call reports failure as `InvalidHandleValue`, which is
`-1` cast to a pointer, while an allocation-returning one reports it as null. Testing the wrong one is the classic
Win32 mistake, so each declaration says which it uses.

doc.summary: How many `FileTime` ticks make one second.
doc.markdown:
How many `FileTime` ticks make one second.
A `FileTime` counts 100-nanosecond intervals, so this is ten million. It is the conversion every wall-clock
reading here needs.

doc.summary: Seconds between the `FileTime` epoch of 1601 and the Unix epoch of 1970.
doc.markdown:
Seconds between the `FileTime` epoch of 1601 and the Unix epoch of 1970.
Windows counts from a different year than everything else, and this is what converts between them. The gap
includes the leap days of the intervening centuries, which is why it is not a round number.

items.name: QueryPerformanceCounter
items.signature: pub extern func QueryPerformanceCounter(count: *var int64) -> int32

doc.summary: Reads the monotonic performance counter.
doc.markdown:
Reads the monotonic performance counter.
Writes the current count and returns nonzero. It cannot fail on any system this package supports, and the
count is guaranteed not to go backwards — unlike the wall clock, which can. The unit is whatever
QueryPerformanceFrequency reports and is not seconds.
doc.returns: non-zero on success

items.name: QueryPerformanceFrequency
items.signature: pub extern func QueryPerformanceFrequency(frequency: *var int64) -> int32

doc.summary: Reads how many performance-counter ticks make one second.
doc.markdown:
Reads how many performance-counter ticks make one second.
Fixed while the system runs, so a caller reads it once rather than per measurement.

params.name: frequency
params.markdown: receives the counter's fixed frequency, in counts per second

doc.returns: non-zero on success

doc.summary: Reads the current wall-clock time at the highest resolution the system offers.
doc.markdown:
Reads the current wall-clock time at the highest resolution the system offers.
Writes 100-nanosecond intervals since January 1, 1601 UTC. The plain GetSystemTimeAsFileTime is cheaper and
coarser, advancing only at the scheduler's tick.

doc.summary: Reads the current wall-clock time at the system tick's resolution.
doc.markdown: Reads the current wall-clock time at the system tick's resolution.

doc.summary: The whole 64-bit value a `FileTime` splits across two fields.
doc.markdown:
The whole 64-bit value a `FileTime` splits across two fields.
`time` is borrowed and read, so callers pass the value directly. Win32 splits the count into a high and a low
word because the structure predates 64-bit alignment guarantees; this puts it back together.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: its two halves joined into one count of 100-nanosecond ticks since 1601

doc.markdown: The `CreationDisposition` values exposed by this package.

cases.name: CreateNew
cases.doc: Create the file, and fail with `ERROR_FILE_EXISTS` if the name is taken.

cases.name: CreateAlways
cases.doc:
Create the file, truncating whatever is there. Succeeds either way, and reports `ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS` through
`GetLastError` when it truncated rather than created.

cases.name: OpenExisting
cases.doc: Open the file, and fail with `ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND` if it is not there.

cases.name: OpenAlways
cases.doc:
Open the file, creating it if it is not there. Reports `ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS` when it opened rather than
created.

cases.name: TruncateExisting
cases.doc: Open the file and truncate it, failing if it is not there. Needs write access.

doc.summary: `BCRYPT_USE_SYSTEM_PREFERRED_RNG`: draw from the system's preferred generator rather than a named algorithm.
doc.markdown:
`BCRYPT_USE_SYSTEM_PREFERRED_RNG`: draw from the system's preferred generator rather than a named algorithm.
Passed with a null algorithm handle, which is what makes this a one-call interface: nothing has to be opened,
configured, or closed.

doc.summary: `STATUS_SUCCESS`: the status an `NtStatus`-reporting call gives when it worked.
doc.markdown: `STATUS_SUCCESS`: the status an `NtStatus`-reporting call gives when it worked.

items.name: GetRandom
items.signature: pub func GetRandom(buffer: *var opaque, length: uint) -> bool

doc.summary: Fills `length` bytes of `buffer` with unpredictable bytes.
doc.markdown:
Fills `length` bytes of `buffer` with unpredictable bytes.
`buffer` is borrowed and written; `length` is read by value. Returns true when the whole buffer was filled, and
false when the provider refused — there is no partial success to handle, unlike every Unix source.
Runs in time proportional to `length` and allocates nothing.
`buffer` must be writable for `length` bytes. `length` is passed as a 32-bit count, so a request above four
gigabytes is refused rather than truncated.
doc.returns: whether the whole buffer was filled; there is no partial success

doc.summary: `ERROR_SUCCESS`: the operation succeeded, which is the value `GetLastError` reports when nothing has failed.
doc.markdown: `ERROR_SUCCESS`: the operation succeeded, which is the value `GetLastError` reports when nothing has failed.

doc.summary: `ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND`: the named file does not exist.
doc.markdown: `ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND`: the named file does not exist.

doc.summary: `ERROR_PATH_NOT_FOUND`: a directory along the path does not exist.
doc.markdown: `ERROR_PATH_NOT_FOUND`: a directory along the path does not exist.

doc.summary: `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED`: the caller does not have the rights the operation needs.
doc.markdown:
`ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED`: the caller does not have the rights the operation needs.
Also what a sharing violation looks like when the file is already open without the matching share mode.

doc.summary: `ERROR_INVALID_HANDLE`: the handle is not one this operation can use.
doc.markdown: `ERROR_INVALID_HANDLE`: the handle is not one this operation can use.

doc.summary: `ERROR_NOT_ENOUGH_MEMORY`: not enough storage to complete the operation.
doc.markdown:
`ERROR_NOT_ENOUGH_MEMORY`: not enough storage to complete the operation.
Distinct from `ERROR_OUTOFMEMORY`, and which of the two a call reports is the call's own business, so a caller
checking for exhaustion has to accept either.

doc.summary: `ERROR_OUTOFMEMORY`: not enough storage to complete the operation.
doc.markdown: `ERROR_OUTOFMEMORY`: not enough storage to complete the operation.

doc.summary: `ERROR_NOT_SUPPORTED`: the operation is not supported on this object or this system.
doc.markdown: `ERROR_NOT_SUPPORTED`: the operation is not supported on this object or this system.

doc.summary: `ERROR_FILE_EXISTS`: the file already exists, and the call was told not to replace it.
doc.markdown: `ERROR_FILE_EXISTS`: the file already exists, and the call was told not to replace it.

doc.summary: `ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER`: an argument is not valid.
doc.markdown: `ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER`: an argument is not valid.

doc.summary: `ERROR_DISK_FULL`: the volume has no room left.
doc.markdown: `ERROR_DISK_FULL`: the volume has no room left.

doc.summary: `ERROR_PRIVILEGE_NOT_HELD`: the account lacks a privilege the operation requires.
doc.markdown:
`ERROR_PRIVILEGE_NOT_HELD`: the account lacks a privilege the operation requires.
What refuses `CreateSymbolicLinkW` on a machine without Developer Mode, where creating a symbolic link needs
`SeCreateSymbolicLinkPrivilege` — a restriction no other supported system places on the same operation.

doc.summary: `ERROR_NO_MORE_FILES`: a directory enumeration has handed over its last entry.
doc.markdown:
`ERROR_NO_MORE_FILES`: a directory enumeration has handed over its last entry.
Reported by `FindNextFileW` at the end of an enumeration, where nothing has gone wrong at all — the caller
distinguishes it from a real failure by this code.

doc.summary: `ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS`: the object already exists.
doc.markdown:
`ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS`: the object already exists.
Reported by `CreateDirectoryW` where `ERROR_FILE_EXISTS` is reported by the file calls, which is why a caller
asking "was it already there" has to accept both.

doc.summary: `ERROR_INVALID_ADDRESS`: the address is not one the operation can use.
doc.markdown: `ERROR_INVALID_ADDRESS`: the address is not one the operation can use.

doc.summary: `ERROR_COMMITMENT_LIMIT`: the system's commit limit is reached, so nothing more can be backed.
doc.markdown:
`ERROR_COMMITMENT_LIMIT`: the system's commit limit is reached, so nothing more can be backed.
What a large commit fails with when the page file cannot grow, as distinct from running out of address space.

doc.summary: `GENERIC_READ`: the handle may read.
doc.markdown: `GENERIC_READ`: the handle may read.

doc.summary: `GENERIC_WRITE`: the handle may write.
doc.markdown: `GENERIC_WRITE`: the handle may write.

doc.summary: `FILE_APPEND_DATA`: the handle may append, and only append.
doc.markdown:
`FILE_APPEND_DATA`: the handle may append, and only append.
The access right that makes an append-only handle: every write lands at the end whatever the file pointer
says, which `GENERIC_WRITE` does not promise.

doc.summary: `FILE_SHARE_READ`: other openers may read while this handle is open.
doc.markdown:
`FILE_SHARE_READ`: other openers may read while this handle is open.
Windows denies sharing by default, which is the opposite of every Unix. A file opened without this cannot be
opened for reading by anything else, including the same process.

doc.summary: `FILE_SHARE_WRITE`: other openers may write while this handle is open.
doc.markdown: `FILE_SHARE_WRITE`: other openers may write while this handle is open.

doc.summary: `FILE_SHARE_DELETE`: the file may be renamed or deleted while this handle is open.
doc.markdown: `FILE_SHARE_DELETE`: the file may be renamed or deleted while this handle is open.

doc.summary: `FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL`: no attributes beyond being an ordinary file.
doc.markdown: `FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL`: no attributes beyond being an ordinary file.

doc.summary: `FILE_ATTRIBUTE_READONLY`: the file may not be opened for writing or deleted.
doc.markdown:
`FILE_ATTRIBUTE_READONLY`: the file may not be opened for writing or deleted.
The whole of Windows' permission model as this package uses it: there are ACLs underneath, but nothing in the
portable surface can express them, and this bit is what `chmod` maps onto.

doc.summary: `FILE_ATTRIBUTE_DIRECTORY`: the name is a directory.
doc.markdown: `FILE_ATTRIBUTE_DIRECTORY`: the name is a directory.

doc.summary: `FILE_ATTRIBUTE_REPARSE_POINT`: the name carries a reparse point, which is what a symbolic link is.
doc.markdown: `FILE_ATTRIBUTE_REPARSE_POINT`: the name carries a reparse point, which is what a symbolic link is.

doc.summary: `INVALID_FILE_ATTRIBUTES`: what `GetFileAttributesW` returns when it could not answer.
doc.markdown: `INVALID_FILE_ATTRIBUTES`: what `GetFileAttributesW` returns when it could not answer.

doc.summary: `FILE_FLAG_BACKUP_SEMANTICS`: let `CreateFileW` open a directory.
doc.markdown:
`FILE_FLAG_BACKUP_SEMANTICS`: let `CreateFileW` open a directory.
Without it a directory cannot be opened at all, which makes this the flag every metadata query needs.

doc.summary: `FILE_FLAG_OPEN_REPARSE_POINT`: open the symbolic link itself rather than what it points at.
doc.markdown: `FILE_FLAG_OPEN_REPARSE_POINT`: open the symbolic link itself rather than what it points at.

doc.summary: `FILE_FLAG_DELETE_ON_CLOSE`: remove the file when its last handle closes.
doc.markdown: `FILE_FLAG_DELETE_ON_CLOSE`: remove the file when its last handle closes.

doc.summary: `FILE_FLAG_WRITE_THROUGH`: writes reach the device before the call returns.
doc.markdown: `FILE_FLAG_WRITE_THROUGH`: writes reach the device before the call returns.

doc.summary: `SYMBOLIC_LINK_FLAG_DIRECTORY`: the link's target is a directory.
doc.markdown:
`SYMBOLIC_LINK_FLAG_DIRECTORY`: the link's target is a directory.
Windows types its symbolic links: a link made without this flag misbehaves when its target is a directory,
which no Unix symlink ever asked anyone to know in advance.

doc.summary:
`SYMBOLIC_LINK_FLAG_ALLOW_UNPRIVILEGED_CREATE`: let a Developer Mode machine create the link without the
privilege older systems demand.
doc.markdown:
`SYMBOLIC_LINK_FLAG_ALLOW_UNPRIVILEGED_CREATE`: let a Developer Mode machine create the link without the
privilege older systems demand.
Harmless where the privilege is held; without Developer Mode or the privilege the call still fails with
`ERROR_PRIVILEGE_NOT_HELD`.

doc.summary: `MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING`: let the move overwrite an existing target.
doc.markdown: `MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING`: let the move overwrite an existing target.

doc.summary: `MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH`: do not return until the move has reached the disk.
doc.markdown:
`MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH`: do not return until the move has reached the disk.
With `MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING`, this is what makes publishing a file under its final name durable.

doc.summary: Creates or opens a file or device, taking a UTF-16 path.
doc.markdown:
Creates or opens a file or device, taking a UTF-16 path.
Returns InvalidHandleValue on failure, not null. The share mode is not a default: passing zero denies every
other opener, which is Windows' behaviour and not most callers' intent.

offset 0 (4 bytes), three FILETIMEs from 4, the size's halves at 28 and 32, and the entry's NUL-terminated

doc.summary: Fills a BY_HANDLE_FILE_INFORMATION record for an open handle.
doc.markdown:
Fills a BY_HANDLE_FILE_INFORMATION record for an open handle.
The record is 52 bytes: attributes at offset 0 (4 bytes), the creation, last-access and last-write
FILETIMEs at 4, 12 and 20 (8 bytes each), the volume serial number at 28, the size's high and low halves

doc.summary: `MEM_COMMIT`: back the range with storage.
doc.markdown: `MEM_COMMIT`: back the range with storage.

doc.summary: `MEM_RESERVE`: take the address space without backing it.
doc.markdown:
`MEM_RESERVE`: take the address space without backing it.
A reserved page cannot be touched. Touching one faults exactly as an unmapped page does, which is what makes
reservation a cheap way to hold a range for later.

doc.summary: `MEM_RESET`: the contents are no longer of interest and need not be written to the page file.
doc.markdown: `MEM_RESET`: the contents are no longer of interest and need not be written to the page file.

doc.summary: `MEM_RELEASE`: give back the whole reservation, which `VirtualFree` requires a size of zero for.
doc.markdown: `MEM_RELEASE`: give back the whole reservation, which `VirtualFree` requires a size of zero for.

doc.summary: `MEM_DECOMMIT`: take back the storage but keep the reservation.
doc.markdown: `MEM_DECOMMIT`: take back the storage but keep the reservation.

doc.summary: `PAGE_NOACCESS`: the pages may not be touched at all.
doc.markdown: `PAGE_NOACCESS`: the pages may not be touched at all.

doc.summary: `PAGE_READONLY`: the pages may be read.
doc.markdown: `PAGE_READONLY`: the pages may be read.

doc.summary: `PAGE_READWRITE`: the pages may be read and written.
doc.markdown: `PAGE_READWRITE`: the pages may be read and written.

doc.summary: `PAGE_EXECUTE`: the pages may be executed.
doc.markdown: `PAGE_EXECUTE`: the pages may be executed.

doc.summary: `PAGE_EXECUTE_READ`: the pages may be executed and read.
doc.markdown: `PAGE_EXECUTE_READ`: the pages may be executed and read.

doc.summary: `PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE`: the pages may be executed, read and written.
doc.markdown:
`PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE`: the pages may be executed, read and written.
What a hardened process refuses, and what an exploit needs. Prefer writing through one protection and executing
through another.

doc.summary: `PAGE_GUARD`: the next touch raises a one-shot guard exception and then clears the flag.
doc.markdown:
`PAGE_GUARD`: the next touch raises a one-shot guard exception and then clears the flag.
Combined with another protection. This is how a stack grows on Windows.

doc.summary: Locks a region into physical memory so it is never written to the page file.
doc.markdown:
Locks a region into physical memory so it is never written to the page file.
The way to keep a secret off the disk. The process working-set limit bounds how much may be locked, so this
fails for a large region rather than succeeding slowly.
doc.returns: non-zero on success

doc.summary: An opaque kernel object reference.
doc.markdown:
An opaque kernel object reference.
Pointer-sized and owned by the kernel. A handle is valid until `CloseHandle` takes it, after which the number may
be reused by the next object opened — so a stale handle does not fail, it addresses something else.

doc.summary: A module reference, as `LoadLibraryW` returns one.
doc.markdown: A module reference, as `LoadLibraryW` returns one.

doc.summary: Win32's `BOOL`: a 32-bit integer where zero is false and anything else is true.
doc.markdown:
Win32's `BOOL`: a 32-bit integer where zero is false and anything else is true.
Not a one-byte boolean, and not `bool`. A call returning one reports failure as zero and success as anything
else, which is why comparing against `1` is wrong.

doc.summary: Win32's `DWORD`: a 32-bit unsigned integer.
doc.markdown: Win32's `DWORD`: a 32-bit unsigned integer.

doc.summary: A UTF-16 code unit, which is what every `*W` entry point takes.
doc.markdown:
A UTF-16 code unit, which is what every `*W` entry point takes.
Not a character: a scalar outside the basic plane occupies two of these.

doc.summary: An `NTSTATUS`: the status code the native and cryptographic interfaces report with.
doc.markdown:
An `NTSTATUS`: the status code the native and cryptographic interfaces report with.
Zero and above is success; below zero is failure. This is a different scheme from `GetLastError`, and a value of
one must never be read as the other.

doc.summary: The value a handle-returning call reports failure with.
doc.markdown:
The value a handle-returning call reports failure with.
`-1` cast to a pointer, which is not null. `CreateFileW` and `FindFirstFileW` report failure this way; a
memory-returning call such as `VirtualAlloc` reports null instead.

doc.summary: Win32's `FILETIME`: a count of 100-nanosecond ticks since the start of 1601, UTC.
doc.markdown:
Win32's `FILETIME`: a count of 100-nanosecond ticks since the start of 1601, UTC.
Split across two 32-bit halves because the record predates a 64-bit integer being ordinary, and the halves are
not aligned as one — `FileTimeTicks` joins them, and reading the pair as a `uint64` is what a caller must not do.
The epoch is not the Unix one. `FileTimeToUnixEpochSeconds` is the difference.

fields.name: lowDateTime
fields.doc: The low 32 bits of the tick count.

fields.name: highDateTime
fields.doc: The high 32 bits of the tick count.

doc.summary: Win32's `SYSTEMTIME`: a broken-down date and time, one field per component.
doc.markdown:
Win32's `SYSTEMTIME`: a broken-down date and time, one field per component.
Whether it is UTC or local time is decided by the call that filled it, not by the record — `GetSystemTime` gives
one and `GetLocalTime` the other, and nothing here distinguishes them afterwards.
The fields are private: `Rux/Time` is the calendar interface, and this exists so a Win32 signature can name the
record it takes.

doc.summary: Win32's `WIN32_FIND_DATAA`: one directory entry, as `FindFirstFileA` and `FindNextFileA` fill it.
doc.markdown:
Win32's `WIN32_FIND_DATAA`: one directory entry, as `FindFirstFileA` and `FindNextFileA` fill it.
The narrow form, whose names come through the process code page and so cannot express every name a file system
can hold. `Rux/FileSystem` enumerates through the wide entry points instead; this is here so a caller reaching
for the `A` family directly can name the record they take.
The fields are private: the layout is Microsoft's and reading it is the enumerating code's business.

doc.summary: What `GetSystemInfo` reports about the machine.
doc.markdown:
What `GetSystemInfo` reports about the machine.
The two granularities are not the same and the difference matters: `pageSize` is what protection is applied at,
while `allocationGranularity` is what a reservation's base address is rounded to, and on every Windows release it
is 64 KiB rather than a page. A reservation therefore wastes address space that a page-granular system would not.

fields.name: processorArchitecture
fields.doc: The processor architecture, or a union member on the oldest releases; not read by this package.

fields.name: pageSize
fields.doc: The size of a page, which is what memory protection is applied at.

fields.name: minimumApplicationAddress
fields.doc: The lowest address an application may have.

fields.name: maximumApplicationAddress
fields.doc: The highest address an application may have.

fields.name: activeProcessorMask
fields.doc: A mask of the processors this process may run on.

fields.name: numberOfProcessors
fields.doc: How many logical processors the machine has.

fields.name: processorType
fields.doc: The processor type, obsolete and not read by this package.

fields.name: allocationGranularity
fields.doc: The granularity a reservation's base address is rounded to, which is not the page size.
